title: Red sprites
hook: Giant red flashes flicker high above storms, and science missed them until 1989.
peek: High above big thunderstorms, huge red flashes shaped like jellyfish and carrots flicker for a split second. Pilots had told of them for decades, but scientists only confirmed them in 1989, when a camera test caught one by chance.
lede: Above some large thunderstorms, far higher than normal lightning, enormous red flashes appear for a few thousandths of a second. They can be tens of kilometres across and reach about 90 km up. Pilots had described them for decades, but many scientists doubted the reports. Then in 1989 a camera being tested for something else caught one.

bullets.text: In July 1989 a team led by John Winckler at the University of Minnesota was testing a low-light camera for a rocket flight. Reviewing the footage, they found two bright columns of light above distant storm clouds.
Sprites happen in thin air between about 50 and 90 km up. There, an electrical surge from a strong lightning strike below excites nitrogen gas, which glows red.
Sprites come in shapes that scientists name by eye: columns, carrots with trailing tendrils, and wide jellyfish forms with a red top and tendrils hanging down.
The name sprite, after the airy spirits in Shakespeare, was chosen partly because it did not imply any theory about how they worked.
Astronauts on the International Space Station have photographed sprites from above, and amateur photographers now catch them from the ground with sensitive cameras aimed over distant storms.
